summary: Empty parts of the atlas held many histories that had not yet been entered. This campaign adds named places and dated activity across six western U.S. areas, coastal Louisiana and the Gilbert, Phoenix and Line islands. It brings in archaeological buildings and camps, enduring Indigenous communities, colonial labor, commerce, warfare and documented local departures.
continuity: A place can have people before and after a poorly documented interval. The map keeps its earlier evidence visible rather than turning that gap into a disappearance. Where community histories support continuing habitation, the inhabited-place record spans the interval. Where they do not, the marker stays as earlier evidence and the later activity remains separately dated. A dated sample is not the date everybody arrived or left. Explicitly documented closure or relocation receives a separate cue: for example, the U.S. Army leaving Fort Phil Kearny in 1868, or Kiritimati’s 1905–1912 occupation gap. Neither a government incorporation date nor the atlas endpoint means the first or last human presence.

regions.Idaho — southern / central: Owl Cave records bison processing near the end of the Ice Age. Much later, Bison Rockshelter preserves a Shoshonean tool tradition. Fort Hall connects two different places: a fur-trade post on the Snake River and the later Shoshone–Bannock reservation community. The post’s closure did not end the people’s history.
regions.Montana — central / eastern plains: Bergstrom preserves repeated communal bison hunts, separated in the ground by layers and dates. Fort Benton later linked Blackfeet robe trading to the Missouri River. Little Bighorn and the establishment of Fort Belknap bring warfare and imposed land changes into the nineteenth-century map.
regions.Nevada — central / eastern basins: Bonneville Estates Rockshelter records repeated visits over thousands of years. Baker Village adds farming, houses and storage near the Snake Range. Ruby Valley treaty proceedings and the Elko Colony show Western Shoshone history continuing through a period of restricted land and changing government.
regions.Nevada — southern desert: Corn Creek’s houses, hearths and crops show people returning to the springs across many periods. Big Springs adds a partly underground Puebloan house, and Mount Irish combines camps with rock art. Later Moapa and Las Vegas Paiute records show enduring communities and the shrinking land bases imposed on them.
regions.Wyoming — eastern plains: Powars II was a source of red pigment. Hell Gap and Vore preserve different forms of recurring activity: camp life and collective bison hunting. Fort Phil Kearny and the Fort Laramie treaty place the struggle over the Bozeman Trail on the same shared clock.
regions.Wyoming — western mountains: Fishing Bridge and High Rise Village show how people used mountain environments, including hearths and high-elevation lodges. The Fort Bridger treaty and Wind River records follow Eastern Shoshone and Northern Arapaho histories into the reservation period. A reservation reference point is not a reconstruction of each family’s camp.
regions.Louisiana — western coastal plain: On coastal ridges, Veazey’s pottery and Morgan’s mound-top building reveal organized places in a marsh landscape. Chitimacha continuity at Charenton sits beside the colonial growth of Nueva Iberia and St. Martinville. Archaeology at Avery Island follows enslaved households and later African American workers, while Lake Charles grows with lumber and transport.
regions.Kiribati — Gilbert Islands: At Buota, plant remains and garden soils connect people with swamp-taro cultivation. Later accounts locate villages, chiefly courts, churches and trading stores at Koinawa, Binoinano and Butaritari. The Alexa’s service connects Butaritari’s copra economy with supplies and passengers from Australia.
regions.Kiribati — Phoenix Islands: Manra’s fishhooks and imported Samoan basalt, and Orona’s cooking mound, establish human activity centuries before the guano companies. Historical labor camps and coconut planting then create a separate island story. We know earlier communities departed before later visitors found the islands empty, but the checked evidence does not fix when or why.
regions.Kiribati — Line Islands: Kiritimati’s archaeological complexes and Tabuaeran’s imported Marquesan adze show earlier island connections. Nineteenth-century plantations, harbor settlements and the cable station bring workers and families into view. Kiritimati’s documented 1905–1912 gap is retained, followed by the renewed estate from 1913; it is not treated like an unexplored archaeological interval.

held.title: Celebration Park (Warick site)
held.reason: The excavated site has Middle and Late Archaic diagnostics. The cited park report does not establish secure absolute bounds for the layers, and visitor-page petroglyph estimates cannot substitute.

held.title: Wahkpa Chu’gn buffalo jump
held.reason: Montana's public interpretation reports an approximate 2,000 BP onset and identifies Besant, Avonlea and Old Women’s/Saddle Butte use. This source does not resolve site-specific calibrated ages for the separate phases.

held.title: Pictograph Cave
held.reason: The park reports an approximately 9,000-year-old projectile point, a 2,145-year-old pigment measurement and much later painted guns, but the available park account does not show calibrated ages or uncertainty. Scott, Davis and Adovasio (2014), doi:10.1179/2052546X13Y.0000000001, directly dated four objects to the Late Prehistoric period. Exact lab windows remain to be verified.

held.title: Obsidian Cliff quarry
held.reason: NPS places first obsidian quarrying more than 11,000 years ago. An exact earliest window cannot be inferred from the lower bound. Ohio Hopewell obsidian provenance is valuable evidence for a later mapped exchange endpoint if directly dated contexts are available.

held.title: Mummy Cave (North Fork Shoshone)
held.reason: Original abstract says the record begins more than 9,000 years ago. Seek dated stratigraphic components and calibrate legacy radiocarbon assays before mapping numeric windows.

held.title: Medicine Lodge Creek archaeological site
held.reason: State archaeological synthesis reports habitation dating back about 10,000 years, without giving a specific archaeological sample or diagnostic age. Hold for detailed chronology. Rock-art dates must be independent of tool dates.

held.title: Te Bakoa, Nikunau
held.reason: Full text with sample identifiers, age distributions, and oven locations. Do not transfer the islet proxy to Rungata or establish uninterrupted occupation.

held.title: Utiroa, Makin
held.reason: Read primary excavation text or find an adequate published contextual table.

held.title: Bear River Massacre
held.reason: Already mapped as violence-bear-river-1863. The new research points to the same event, so it is not added as a second marker.

held.title: Later Veazey occupation
held.reason: Excavation separates the early Marksville component from later pottery. The later component needs its own supported date before it can extend the local timeline.

spatialPolicy: Use public locality references with their actual precision. Restricted sites and unidentified buildings are not assigned invented excavation coordinates. Broad atoll references are labeled as such. Separate phases of the same known place reuse its identity; a historic plantation is not placed at a prehistoric workshop merely because both were on one island.
reuse: Original historical summaries, with linked primary and institutional sources. No third-party illustrations or copied passages added. The atlas license does not override source-specific rights.
